questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.1
questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When exact extent cannot be determined directly, weigh outcome-specific follow-up accounting and other source-supported information for a probably yes or probably no judgment. If the extent remains unknown because that evidence does not support a reasonable inference, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement. Outcome-specific observed/expected follow-up time can inform a probable judgment, but is not a participant-observation fraction; vital status alone does not ascertain nonfatal components. Explain what the evidence implies about missing outcomes for the approved estimate.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when neither direct nor indirect evidence supports a reasonable judgment about availability after bounded retrieval. Imprecise quantification alone does not require no_information. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

answer_anchors.text: Outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
Outcome data were not available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
The report provides no information about the extent of missing outcome data.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Where follow-up is incomplete, explain why the unobserved outcomes plausibly could or could not make an important difference to the approved estimate, rather than citing a small percentage alone. Relate the reported extent to the outcome event scale or variability and any known follow-up timing or reasons; retain what is unknown. For time-to-event estimates, event counts contextualize scale but do not by themselves mathematically bound the hazard ratio or its interval. A calibrated probable judgment can rest on nearly complete outcome accounting without exact censoring times or a formal sensitivity analysis. Missing reasons or timing alone do not require no_information; judge whether available circumstances support a reasonable inference.

questions.wording: If N/PN/NI to 3.1: Is there evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data?
questions.official_guidance: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance p. 45, Box 8, signalling question 3.2
questions.bias_construct: Whether there is evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data.
questions.decision_rule: Evidence may come from methods correcting for bias or sensitivity analyses showing little change under plausible assumptions about missingness and true outcome. The assumptions must match the documented missingness mechanism and the approved Result. A comparison that changes group attribution, such as ITT versus as-treated, does not test unobserved outcome values unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship. Last-observation-carried-forward or multiple imputation based only on intervention group should not be assumed to correct bias.
evidence_needed: A bias-correcting analysis or sensitivity analysis with plausible missingness assumptions and its result, including the missingness mechanism it addresses.
If the source only changes intervention-group attribution or analysis membership, record that distinction; do not describe it as a test of unobserved outcome values without source support.
questions.no_information_rule: No_information is not an allowed response to this question in the parallel-assignment pack. Answer no/probably no when inspected evidence does not establish protection from missing-data bias. No does not assert that bias occurred: retain source coverage limits and unknown missingness mechanisms. Ground the scoped negative answer in inspected Evidence or a valid scoped no-hit receipt; an unsupported limitation alone is insufficient.

The available evidence does not show that the result was free from missing-data bias.

considerations: Imputation alone is not evidence that missing outcome data did not bias the result.

Availability and mitigation are separate premises: a familiar method name or numerically stable estimate is not enough; the sensitivity analysis must span plausible assumptions relevant to the documented missingness mechanism.
This question permits complete ascertainment, mechanism-matched reassurance, and legitimate uncertainty. Do not apply a universal percentage threshold in place of a Result-specific impact judgment.

questions.wording: If N/PN to 3.2: Could missingness in the outcome depend on its true value?
questions.official_guidance: If loss to follow up, or withdrawal from the study, could be related to participants’ health status, then it is possible that missingness in the outcome was influenced by its true value. However, if all missing outcome data occurred for documented reasons that are unrelated to the outcome then the risk of bias due to missing outcome data will be low.

questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness in the outcome could depend on its true value.
questions.decision_rule: Answer yes or probably yes when loss to follow-up or withdrawal could relate to health status or outcome. Answer no or probably no when all missingness had documented reasons unrelated to outcome, such as a failed measuring device or interruption to routine data collection.
evidence_needed: Reasons for missingness and their relationship to participants' health status or true outcome, including censoring and treatment switching in time-to-event analyses.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when the reasons for missingness do not permit assessment of dependence on the true value.

answer_anchors.text: Missingness could depend on the true outcome value.
Documented missingness reasons are unrelated to the outcome.

considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation is not loss to follow-up when outcome ascertainment continues; stopping treatment or an analysis label alone does not establish whether the outcome was observed. Last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.

Withdrawal or censoring after worsening health or symptoms can support possible dependence on the outcome value when the source links the reason to that participant's outcome; stopping treatment without that follow-up loss does not.
invalid_shortcuts: a reason for withdrawal without its relation to outcome

questions.wording: If Y/PY/NI to 3.3: Is it likely that missingness in the outcome depended on its true value?
questions.official_guidance: This question distinguishes between situations in which (i) missingness could depend on its true value and (ii) it is likely that missingness depended on its true value. Five reasons for answering ‘Yes’ are differences between intervention groups in the proportions of missing outcome data; reported reasons that provide evidence that missingness depends on its true value; reasons that differ between intervention groups; trial circumstances; and censoring when participants stop or change their assigned intervention.
questions.source_locator: Full guidance pp. 45-46, Box 8, signalling question 3.4
questions.bias_construct: Whether missingness that could depend on true value likely depended on it.
questions.decision_rule: Consider differences in missingness or censoring rates, reasons that depend on true value, reasons differing between groups, trial circumstances, and censoring after stopping or changing intervention. Answer no when analysis accounted for participant characteristics likely to explain the relationship.
evidence_needed: Group-specific missingness or censoring, reasons for missingness, trial circumstances, and any analysis accounting for relevant participant characteristics.
questions.no_information_rule: Use no_information when likelihood of dependence on true value cannot be judged from the available evidence.

answer_anchors.text: Missingness likely depended on the true outcome value.
The analysis accounted for characteristics explaining the relationship, or dependence was not likely.

considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Weigh evidence for and against likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances, including comparable outcome follow-up and continued ascertainment after treatment stopping. Such contextual counterevidence is not proof of non-informative censoring; absence of precise reasons or timing alone does not require no_information, and absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.

Full guidance section 6.1, p. 39 distinguishes genuinely missing measurements (D3) from available outcomes deliberately excluded from analysis (D2). Outcome-driven rescue, switching, or post-change analysis exclusion does not by itself establish non-observation; scheduled collection does not establish observation either. Link the outcome-related reason to actual missing measurements or missing follow-up before treating it as a D3 mechanism. If that link is unknown, retain it as an unresolved premise rather than assigning analysis exclusions to missingness.

Paired control: after the same outcome-driven treatment change, endpoint measurements collected but omitted from analysis raise an assignment-analysis concern in D2; measurements not obtained require D3 appraisal. If collection is only planned or unspecified, observed availability remains unknown. Differences in rescue rates alone are not differences in missing-outcome rates. Compare post-change handling with the approved assignment target; matching endpoint and time point alone does not establish the same estimand.

a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised,
adaptive Bayesian trial
Tom P Freeman, Chandni Hindocha, Gianluca Baio, Natacha D C Shaban, Emily M Thomas, Danica Astbury, Abigail M Freeman, Rachel Lees,
Sam Craft, Paul D Morrison, Michael A P Bloomfield, Dominic O'Ryan, Jane Kinghorn, Celia J A Morgan, Ali Mofeez, H Valerie Curran
Summary
Background A substantial and unmet clinical need exists for pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.
Cannabidiol could offer a novel treatment, but it is unclear which doses might be efficacious or safe. Therefore, we
aimed to identify efficacious doses and eliminate inefficacious doses in a phase 2a trial using an adaptive Bayesian design.
Methods We did a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, adaptive Bayesian trial at the Clinical
Psychopharmacology Unit (University College London, London, UK). We used an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding
design to identify efficacious or inefficacious doses at a-priori interim and final analysis stages. Participants meeting
cannabis use disorder criteria from DSM-5 were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) in the first stage of the trial to
4-week treatment with three different doses of oral cannabidiol (200 mg, 400 mg, or 800 mg) or with matched placebo
during a cessation attempt by use of a double-blinded block randomisation sequence. All participants received a brief
psychological intervention of motivational interviewing. For the second stage of the trial, new participants were
randomly assigned to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim analysis. The primary objective was
to identify the most efficacious dose of cannabidiol for reducing cannabis use. The primary endpoints were lower
urinary 11-nor-9-carboxy-δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC-COOH):creatinine ratio, increased days per week with
abstinence from cannabis during treatment, or both, evidenced by posterior probabilities that cannabidiol is better
than placebo exceeding 0·9. All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. This trial is registered with
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02044809) and the EU Clinical Trials Register (2013-000361-36).
Findings Between May 28, 2014, and Aug 12, 2015 (first stage), 48 participants were randomly assigned to
placebo (n=12) and to cannabidiol 200 mg (n=12), 400 mg (n=12), and 800 mg (n=12). At interim analysis, cannabidiol
200 mg was eliminated from the trial as an inefficacious dose. Between May 24, 2016, and Jan 12, 2017 (second stage),
randomisation continued and an additional 34 participants were allocated (1:1:1) to cannabidiol 400 mg (n=12),
cannabidiol 800 mg (n=11), and placebo (n=11). At final analysis, cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded primary
endpoint criteria (0·9) for both primary outcomes. For urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, the probability of being the
most efficacious dose compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9995 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9965
for cannabidiol 800 mg. For days with abstinence from cannabis, the probability of being the most efficacious dose
compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9966 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9247 for cannabidiol 800 mg.
Compared with placebo, cannabidiol 400 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -94·21 ng/mL (95% interval
estimate -161·83 to -35·56) and increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·48 days per week (0·15 to 0·82). Compared
with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -72·02 ng/mL (-135·47 to -19·52) and
increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·27 days per week (-0·09 to 0·64). Cannabidiol was well tolerated, with no
severe adverse events recorded, and 77 (94%) of 82 participants completed treatment.
Interpretation In the first randomised clinical trial of cannabidiol for cannabis use disorder, cannabidiol 400 mg and
800 mg were safe and more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

sections.excerpt: Evidence that the result was not biased by missing outcome data may come from analysis methods that correct for bias, or sensitivity analyses showing that results are little changed under a range of plausible assumptions about the relationship between missingness in the outcome and its true value. However, imputing the outcome variable, either through methods such as ‘last-observation-carried-forward’ or via multiple imputation based only on intervention group, should not be assumed to correct for bias due to missing outcome data.

63|a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised,
64|adaptive Bayesian trial
65|Tom P Freeman, Chandni Hindocha, Gianluca Baio, Natacha D C Shaban, Emily M Thomas, Danica Astbury, Abigail M Freeman, Rachel Lees,

67|Summary
68|Background A substantial and unmet clinical need exists for pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.
69|Cannabidiol could offer a novel treatment, but it is unclear which doses might be efficacious or safe. Therefore, we
70|aimed to identify efficacious doses and eliminate inefficacious doses in a phase 2a trial using an adaptive Bayesian design.
71|Methods We did a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, adaptive Bayesian trial at the Clinical
72|Psychopharmacology Unit (University College London, London, UK). We used an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding
73|design to identify efficacious or inefficacious doses at a-priori interim and final analysis stages. Participants meeting
74|cannabis use disorder criteria from DSM-5 were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) in the first stage of the trial to
75|4-week treatment with three different doses of oral cannabidiol (200 mg, 400 mg, or 800 mg) or with matched placebo
76|during a cessation attempt by use of a double-blinded block randomisation sequence. All participants received a brief
77|psychological intervention of motivational interviewing. For the second stage of the trial, new participants were
78|randomly assigned to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim analysis. The primary objective was
79|to identify the most efficacious dose of cannabidiol for reducing cannabis use. The primary endpoints were lower
80|urinary 11-nor-9-carboxy-δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC-COOH):creatinine ratio, increased days per week with
81|abstinence from cannabis during treatment, or both, evidenced by posterior probabilities that cannabidiol is better
82|than placebo exceeding 0·9. All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. This trial is registered with
83|ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02044809) and the EU Clinical Trials Register (2013-000361-36).
84|Findings Between May 28, 2014, and Aug 12, 2015 (first stage), 48 participants were randomly assigned to
85|placebo (n=12) and to cannabidiol 200 mg (n=12), 400 mg (n=12), and 800 mg (n=12). At interim analysis, cannabidiol
86|200 mg was eliminated from the trial as an inefficacious dose. Between May 24, 2016, and Jan 12, 2017 (second stage),
87|randomisation continued and an additional 34 participants were allocated (1:1:1) to cannabidiol 400 mg (n=12),
88|cannabidiol 800 mg (n=11), and placebo (n=11). At final analysis, cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded primary
89|endpoint criteria (0·9) for both primary outcomes. For urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, the probability of being the
90|most efficacious dose compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9995 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9965
91|for cannabidiol 800 mg. For days with abstinence from cannabis, the probability of being the most efficacious dose
92|compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9966 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9247 for cannabidiol 800 mg.
93|Compared with placebo, cannabidiol 400 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -94·21 ng/mL (95% interval
94|estimate -161·83 to -35·56) and increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·48 days per week (0·15 to 0·82). Compared
95|with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -72·02 ng/mL (-135·47 to -19·52) and
96|increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·27 days per week (-0·09 to 0·64). Cannabidiol was well tolerated, with no
97|severe adverse events recorded, and 77 (94%) of 82 participants completed treatment.
98|Interpretation In the first randomised clinical trial of cannabidiol for cannabis use disorder, cannabidiol 400 mg and
99|800 mg were safe and more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.

102|Introduction
103|Cannabis is increasingly being legalised for medicinal
104|and recreational use. The long-term effects of these
105|policy reforms are unclear, but might include substantial
106|changes to the types of cannabis products sold and their
107|availability to millions of people worldwide.1 When
108|considering the potential health effects of cannabis use,
109|its largest contribution to the global burden of disease is
110|the impact of cannabis use disorders, which affect an
111|estimated 22 million people worldwide-similar to the
112|prevalence of opioid use disorders.2
113|Δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), a partial cannabinoid
114|receptor agonist, is the primary cannabinoid in cannabis
115|products and causes dose-dependent intoxicating and

29|Despite the substantial and increasing demand for
30|treatment, no pharmacotherapies are recommended for
31|the treatment of cannabis use disorders.11
32|Cannabidiol is another cannabinoid found in many
33|cannabis products.4 Cannabidiol has minimal direct
34|action at cannabinoid receptors but it has broad pharma
35|cological actions, including inhibiting the hydrolysis and
36|reuptake of endocannabinoids12 and negative allosteric
37|modulation of cannabinoid receptors.13 Cannabidiol has
38|generated substantial interest because of its potential
39|medicinal uses14 and ability to interact with the effects of
40|THC.15 Cannabidiol has shown therapeutic effects in
41|humans and preclinical models of addiction by reducing
42|the effect of drug-related cues in attentional bias,16,17
43|cue-induced craving,18 and cue-induced reinstatement19
44|paradigms. Collectively, these studies suggest that canna
45|bidiol has potential for treating a range of substance use
46|disorders including cannabis,16 opioids,18,19 and tobacco.17,20
47|A meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials found that
48|cannabidiol was safe and well tolerated with few adverse
49|effects, but interactions with other medications should
50|be monitored carefully because cannabidiol can inhibit
51|cytochrome P450 enzymes.21
52|To our knowledge, no randomised trials have inves
53|tigated cannabidiol as a potential treatment for cannabis
54|use disorder. Open-label case studies have reported that
55|the use of cannabidiol products was associated with
56|reduced cannabis withdrawal symptoms during cannabis
57|abstinence.22,23 A 10-week open-label trial found that
58|cannabidiol administration was associated with improve
59|ments in psychological wellbeing and cognition in
60|regular users of cannabis who were not engaged in a
61|cessation attempt.24 A combination of THC and canna
62|bidiol at 1:1 ratio (nabiximols) has been found to reduce
63|cannabis withdrawal symptoms, cannabis use, or both in
64|some randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled
65|trials.25-27 However, the causal role of cannabidiol in these
66|studies is unclear because they either used an open-label
67|design22-24 or co-administered THC with cannabidiol.25-27
68|Studies in humans28 and in rat29 models of anxiety
69|have reported inverted-U shaped dose-response effects
70|of cannabidiol. These findings highlight the importance
71|of doing an initial dose-finding trial when investigating
72|a novel indication for cannabidiol. Trials testing a single
73|dose against placebo might not select the most
74|efficacious dose for that indication. Therefore, we did
75|a phase 2a trial to identify potentially efficacious doses
76|and eliminate inefficacious doses using an adaptive
77|Bayesian design. Bayesian methods are advantageous
78|for adaptive clinical trials because of their efficiency,
79|flexibility, and ability to make use of all available
80|evidence in a formal and principled way. As a result,
81|they can reduce the amount of resources and participant
82|burden required when doing clinical trials. Additionally,
83|Bayesian analyses provide direct probabilistic measures
84|of the likelihood of a hypothesis (ie, that a treatment
85|is more efficacious than placebo) given the observed
86|data. As such, they provide results that can be more
87|clinically meaningful than frequentist analyses, which
88|test the likelihood of the observed data given the null
89|hypothesis being true (ie, that a treatment does not
90|differ from placebo). We selected a dose range informed
91|by previous clinical trials of oral cannabidiol30,31
92|of 200 mg, 400 mg, and 800 mg daily for 4 weeks. Our
93|primary objective was to identify which (if any) dose of
94|cannabidiol was most efficacious at reducing cannabis
95|use compared with placebo.
96|Research in context
97|Evidence before the study
98|We searched the Cochrane database and peer-reviewed journal
99|articles in Google Scholar with no language restrictions up to
100|March 12, 2020, using the terms "CBD", "cannabis", and
101|"marijuana". A Cochrane review on pharmacotherapies for
102|cannabis use disorders published in 2019 did not recommend
103|any pharmacotherapies for reducing cannabis use in clinical
104|settings. We found no randomised trials testing cannabidiol
105|as a treatment for cannabis use disorder.
106|Added value of this study
107|To our knowledge, this was the first randomised clinical trial
108|of cannabidiol for the treatment of cannabis use disorder.
109|Using an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding design, we showed
110|that at daily oral doses of 400 mg and 800 mg, cannabidiol
111|was a safe and efficacious treatment for reducing cannabis
112|use in people with a cannabis use disorder, assessed by both
113|biological and self-reported measures.
114|Implications of all the available evidence
115|Cannabidiol at daily oral doses of 400 mg and 800 mg has
116|potential to address the substantial and currently unmet clinical
117|need for a pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.

23|websites, forums, and flyers in the local community. We
24|initially intended to restrict eligibility to individuals aged
25|16-26 years with vital signs in normal limits, but we
26|removed these criteria early in the first stage of the trial to
27|increase the generalisability of our findings to a wider
28|population who might stand to benefit from this
29|treatment. Participants were included if they were aged

38|cannabis in Europe,33 provide a urine sample positive for

40|assessing methamphetamine, cocaine, THC, benzodiaze
41|pines, tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates, phen
42|cyclidine, amphetamines, morphine, and methadone;
43|Alere Toxicology, Abingdon, UK); and have capacity to give

41|Outcomes
42|Primary outcomes were cannabis use, as measured in
43|urine (THC-COOH:creatinine ratio) and by self-report
44|(days per week with abstinence from cannabis). These
45|were the two variables that were most strongly associated
46|with cannabis use disorder severity in a study testing
47|15 different biological and self-reported measures of
48|cannabis use.37 Self-reported days with abstinence from
49|cannabis were assessed weekly by use of the timeline
50|follow-back method.38 The primary endpoints were
51|a reduction in urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, an
52|increase in days per week with abstinence from
53|cannabis, or both for cannabidiol versus placebo during
54|treatment, evidenced by posterior probabilities excee
55|ding 0·9. All primary endpoint data were double entered
56|independently by two researchers (TPF and NDCS for
57|the first stage and EMT and DA for the second stage of
58|the trial) and were 100% verified against source data by
59|an independent clinical trial monitor. Reductions
60|in cannabis use up to the final follow-up were analysed
61|as a secondary endpoint.
62|For secondary outcomes, we assessed the total score
63|of the Cannabis Withdrawal Scale39 and tobacco use,
64|assessed in urine (cotinine:creatinine ratio, lower limit of
65|cotinine quantification 1 ng/mL; ABS Laboratories) and
66|by self-report (number of cigarettes smoked using
67|the timeline follow-back method).38 We assessed alcohol
68|consumption using a timeline follow-back38 of each
69|beverage consumed and its alcohol by volume, which
70|was converted to the number of standard UK alcohol
71|units (8 g alcohol). Sleep quality was assessed by use of
72|the total score on the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index.40
73|Depression and anxiety were assessed by use of total
74|scores on the Beck Depression Inventory41 and Beck
75|Anxiety Inventory.42 Secondary endpoints were reduced
76|cannabis withdrawal symptoms, cigarette and alcohol
77|consumption, urinary cotinine:creatinine ratio, depres
78|sion and anxiety symptoms, and improved sleep quality,
79|assessed during the treatment weeks and up to the
80|final follow-up assessment. Additional secondary out
81|comes included cognitive, biological, and physiological
82|measures that will be reported elsewhere.
83|Participants were asked about possible adverse events
84|at each assessment from week 1 to week 16. Adverse
85|events were categorised as mild (does not interfere
86|with the participant's daily routine and does not require
87|intervention; it causes slight discomfort), moderate
88|(interferes with some aspects of daily routine, or requires
89|intervention, but is not damaging to health; it causes
90|moderate discomfort) or severe (results in alteration,
91|discomfort, or disability that is clearly damaging
92|to health). All adverse events were verified with a medical
93|supervisor and an independent trial monitor throughout
94|the trial on an ongoing basis.
95|Statistical analysis
96|Because no previous trials investigating cannabidiol as
97|a treatment for cannabis use disorder were available, our
98|effect size estimates were informed by a pilot study
99|testing the effects of 1-week treatment with cannabidiol
100|on cigarette consumption in tobacco smokers who
101|intended to quit.20 On the basis of these data, we esti
102|mated that a sample size of 12 participants per group
103|would provide 80% power to detect a similar effect of
104|cannabidiol in this study (Cohen's d 1·21). Because of
105|uncertainty in these estimates, we planned analyses with
106|12 (interim analysis) and 24 participants per group (final
107|analysis) in a two-stage adaptive design.

110|imputation under the assumption of missing at random.

112|from the Bayesian procedure, in accordance with the
113|modelling and distributional assumptions. The same
114|primary endpoints were analysed at interim analysis and

45|Discussion
46|To our knowledge, we did the first randomised clinical
47|trial of cannabidiol for the treatment of cannabis use
48|disorder, in which we used an adaptive Bayesian design
49|to establish which (if any) dose of cannabidiol was more
50|efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use. We
51|eliminated cannabidiol 200 mg at the first stage and
52|continued randomisation to cannabidiol 400 mg, canna
53|bidiol 800 mg, and placebo treatment groups. At final
54|analysis of the primary endpoints, cannabidiol 400 mg
55|and 800 mg were more efficacious than placebo at
56|reducing cannabis use. These treatment effects were
57|found over and above a brief psychological intervention
58|typically delivered in drug treatment settings.
59|All participants in this trial met a DSM-5 diagnosis of
60|cannabis use disorder. Participants expressed a desire to
61|quit using cannabis in the next month, smoked tobacco
62|with their cannabis, and had not succeeded in quitting
63|cannabis use on at least one previous cessation attempt.
64|This is an important population for whom substantial
65|and rising need for treatment exists8,9 and for whom no
66|pharmacotherapies are recommended at present.11
67|Cannabidiol did not differ from placebo in the number of
68|mild or moderate adverse events at 200 mg, 400 mg,
69|or 800 mg doses. No severe adverse events were recorded,
70|and no participants dropped out because of treatment.
71|The excellent safety and tolerability data and exceptionally
72|high retention rates in our trial suggest that these doses
73|of cannabidiol offer a safe and acceptable treatment for
74|this population.
75|To our knowledge, this is the first adaptive Bayesian
76|dose-finding trial of cannabidiol for a new medical
77|indication. The primary objective of this phase 2a trial
78|was to establish which (if any) dose of cannabidiol was
79|more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.
80|Cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded the primary
81|endpoint criterion (posterior probability 0·9) for reducing
82|cannabis use during treatment, with converging evidence
83|from biological and self-reported primary outcomes. Our
84|estimates showed that cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg

91|The effects of the cannabidiol doses tested are suggestive
92|of an inverted-U dose-response curve. The 200 mg group
93|was eliminated as an inefficacious dose, and we found
94|some indication that cannabidiol 400 mg was marginally
95|more efficacious than cannabidiol 800 mg. Secondary
96|endpoints showed that the reductions in cannabis use
97|were maintained up to the final follow-up in the canna
98|bidiol 400 mg group but not in the cannabidiol 800 mg
99|group. From a treatment perspective, our findings indicate
100|that cannabidiol doses ranging from 400 mg to 800 mg
101|have the potential to reduce cannabis use in clinical
102|settings, and that additional benefit is unlikely to be gained
103|from doses exceeding 800 mg. It is important to be aware
104|that this dose range (400 mg to 800 mg) is considerably
105|higher than concentrations found in cannabidiol products
106|widely available without a prescription (eg, 25 mg per
107|day).14 These products have inadequate quality assurance
108|and should not be used for medicinal purposes.

13|with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg reduced cannabis

17|The key strengths of this study include its novel
18|indication, for which substantial clinical need exists, and
19|its adaptive Bayesian dose-finding design. This design
20|enabled us to test a range of doses in an efficient
21|manner, which would have required considerably greater
22|resources and participant burden when using a typical
23|trial design. In terms of limitations, this phase 2a dose-
24|finding trial was not designed to provide robust esti
25|mates of the magnitude of efficacy. Additional evidence is
26|needed to improve the precision of the estimates obtained
27|in this study. Although we found strong evidence for dose-
28|response effects of cannabidiol on plasma cannabidiol
29|concentrations, factors such as food consumption could
30|have contributed to variation in the bioavailability of
31|cannabidiol. This trial used a 4-week treatment period,
32|consistent with a previous clinical trial for psychosis.30

questions.wording: Were data for this outcome available for all, or nearly all, participants randomized?
questions.official_guidance: ‘Nearly all’ should be interpreted as that the number of participants with missing outcome data is sufficiently small that their outcomes, whatever they were, could have made no important difference to the estimated effect of intervention. For continuous outcomes, availability of data from 95% of the participants will often be sufficient. Note that imputed data should be regarded as missing data.

questions.bias_construct: Whether outcome data were available for all or nearly all randomized participants.
questions.decision_rule: Use the randomized population. Yes or probably yes requires evidence that outcome data were available for all or nearly all participants. No or probably no requires evidence of materially incomplete availability. When exact extent cannot be determined directly, weigh outcome-specific follow-up accounting and other source-supported information for a probably yes or probably no judgment. If the extent remains unknown because that evidence does not support a reasonable inference, use no_information. Judge whether the missing outcomes, whatever they were, could make an important difference to this Result; no universal percentage threshold applies. Imputed data count as missing.
evidence_needed: For yes or probably yes, actual outcome-availability evidence can be comparable observed-outcome counts, arm-specific loss-to-follow-up or censoring accounting, or an explicit complete/nearly-complete ascertainment statement. Outcome-specific observed/expected follow-up time can inform a probable judgment, but is not a participant-observation fraction; vital status alone does not ascertain nonfatal components. Explain what the evidence implies about missing outcomes for the approved estimate.

Compare the approved outcome/time point across participant-flow and outcome-data passages. For each comparable arm or unit distinguish the randomized denominator, outcome-observed count, analysed count, imputed count, post-randomization excluded count, and event count. An event count is a numerator, not an outcome-observed count; an analysis denominator is not necessarily an outcome-observed count. Calculate randomized minus observed only when population, arm, unit, and time point are the same. Imputed data count as missing.

Keep outcome availability separate from mitigation quality: a sensitivity analysis or imputation does not change the observed count, and observed cannot be inferred as analysed minus imputed unless the source establishes the same population, time window, and mutually exclusive counts.
questions.no_information_rule: Answer no_information when neither direct nor indirect evidence supports a reasonable judgment about availability after bounded retrieval. Imprecise quantification alone does not require no_information. Lack of evidence for complete availability is not evidence of materially incomplete availability.

considerations: The appropriate population is all randomized participants, not only participants included in a final analysis. Keep outcome availability distinct from exclusions for analysis or conduct; the same passage may inform both Domains for different scientific reasons.

Distinguish administrative censoring at a common data cutoff from censoring caused by missing follow-up; inspect actual rates and follow-up accounting rather than treating a generic censoring rule as outcome-availability evidence.

For time-to-event Results, treatment discontinuation or last-known-alive censoring does not by itself establish that outcome observation stopped; identify the actual observation endpoint, censoring reason, and follow-up pathway. For mortality, recovery or discharge does not establish vital status at a later time point. A total combining completed follow-up, recovery, and death does not establish mortality availability. If availability remains unresolved, inspect outcome-status or missing-value tables, including supplements. Match their outcome and time window to the approved Result. For dichotomous outcomes, compare unknown outcomes with observed events. Recovery may inform bias from missingness, but does not make unknown vital status observed.

Where follow-up is incomplete, explain why the unobserved outcomes plausibly could or could not make an important difference to the approved estimate, rather than citing a small percentage alone. Relate the reported extent to the outcome event scale or variability and any known follow-up timing or reasons; retain what is unknown. For time-to-event estimates, event counts contextualize scale but do not by themselves mathematically bound the hazard ratio or its interval. A calibrated probable judgment can rest on nearly complete outcome accounting without exact censoring times or a formal sensitivity analysis. Missing reasons or timing alone do not require no_information; judge whether available circumstances support a reasonable inference.

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

traps: A no-hit search describes one lexical query, not scientific absence.
A planned method does not prove conduct; a time origin or analysis population does not prove complete follow-up or equal assessment.
An endpoint label or definition does not prove objectivity, blinding, prespecification, or no alternative analyses.
A treatment assignment or visibly different intervention does not by itself prove that participants or personnel knew the assignment.
Different treatment or visit schedules do not by themselves prove that outcome measurement differed between groups.

considerations: For time-to-event outcomes, inspect censoring reasons and timing to identify missing follow-up. A common administrative cutoff does not by itself establish outcome-dependent missingness.

Separate observed outcome data, analysed membership, follow-up availability, and the missingness mechanism. Treatment discontinuation is not loss to follow-up when outcome ascertainment continues; stopping treatment or an analysis label alone does not establish whether the outcome was observed. Last-known-alive censoring is not by itself evidence that observation stopped. This question asks whether the missingness mechanism could depend on the true value; it is not a question about analysis membership.

Withdrawal or censoring after worsening health or symptoms can support possible dependence on the outcome value when the source links the reason to that participant's outcome; stopping treatment without that follow-up loss does not.

considerations: Possible dependence in 3.3 does not establish likely dependence in 3.4. Weigh evidence for and against likelihood from missingness reasons and trial circumstances, including comparable outcome follow-up and continued ascertainment after treatment stopping. Such contextual counterevidence is not proof of non-informative censoring; absence of precise reasons or timing alone does not require no_information, and absent contrary evidence alone does not establish likelihood.

Keep the stages distinct: observed outcome data and follow-up availability describe what was obtained; 3.3 asks whether missingness could depend on the true value; 3.4 asks whether that dependence was likely. Do not promote possible dependence to likely dependence without supporting evidence.

Full guidance section 6.1, p. 39 distinguishes genuinely missing measurements (D3) from available outcomes deliberately excluded from analysis (D2). Outcome-driven rescue, switching, or post-change analysis exclusion does not by itself establish non-observation; scheduled collection does not establish observation either. Link the outcome-related reason to actual missing measurements or missing follow-up before treating it as a D3 mechanism. If that link is unknown, retain it as an unresolved premise rather than assigning analysis exclusions to missingness.

Paired control: after the same outcome-driven treatment change, endpoint measurements collected but omitted from analysis raise an assignment-analysis concern in D2; measurements not obtained require D3 appraisal. Summary
Background A substantial and unmet clinical need exists for pharmacological treatment of cannabis use disorders.
Cannabidiol could offer a novel treatment, but it is unclear which doses might be efficacious or safe. Therefore, we
aimed to identify efficacious doses and eliminate inefficacious doses in a phase 2a trial using an adaptive Bayesian design.
Methods We did a phase 2a, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised, adaptive Bayesian trial at the Clinical
Psychopharmacology Unit (University College London, London, UK). We used an adaptive Bayesian dose-finding
design to identify efficacious or inefficacious doses at a-priori interim and final analysis stages. Participants meeting
cannabis use disorder criteria from DSM-5 were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) in the first stage of the trial to
4-week treatment with three different doses of oral cannabidiol (200 mg, 400 mg, or 800 mg) or with matched placebo
during a cessation attempt by use of a double-blinded block randomisation sequence. All participants received a brief
psychological intervention of motivational interviewing. For the second stage of the trial, new participants were
randomly assigned to placebo or doses deemed efficacious in the interim analysis. The primary objective was
to identify the most efficacious dose of cannabidiol for reducing cannabis use. The primary endpoints were lower
urinary 11-nor-9-carboxy-δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC-COOH):creatinine ratio, increased days per week with
abstinence from cannabis during treatment, or both, evidenced by posterior probabilities that cannabidiol is better
than placebo exceeding 0·9. All analyses were done on an intention-to-treat basis. This trial is registered with
ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02044809) and the EU Clinical Trials Register (2013-000361-36).
Findings Between May 28, 2014, and Aug 12, 2015 (first stage), 48 participants were randomly assigned to
placebo (n=12) and to cannabidiol 200 mg (n=12), 400 mg (n=12), and 800 mg (n=12). At interim analysis, cannabidiol
200 mg was eliminated from the trial as an inefficacious dose. Between May 24, 2016, and Jan 12, 2017 (second stage),
randomisation continued and an additional 34 participants were allocated (1:1:1) to cannabidiol 400 mg (n=12),
cannabidiol 800 mg (n=11), and placebo (n=11). At final analysis, cannabidiol 400 mg and 800 mg exceeded primary
endpoint criteria (0·9) for both primary outcomes. For urinary THC-COOH:creatinine ratio, the probability of being the
most efficacious dose compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9995 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9965
for cannabidiol 800 mg. For days with abstinence from cannabis, the probability of being the most efficacious dose
compared with placebo given the observed data was 0·9966 for cannabidiol 400 mg and 0·9247 for cannabidiol 800 mg.
Compared with placebo, cannabidiol 400 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -94·21 ng/mL (95% interval
estimate -161·83 to -35·56) and increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·48 days per week (0·15 to 0·82). Compared
with placebo, cannabidiol 800 mg decreased THC-COOH:creatinine ratio by -72·02 ng/mL (-135·47 to -19·52) and
increased abstinence from cannabis by 0·27 days per week (-0·09 to 0·64). Cannabidiol was well tolerated, with no
severe adverse events recorded, and 77 (94%) of 82 participants completed treatment.
Interpretation In the first randomised clinical trial of cannabidiol for cannabis use disorder, cannabidiol 400 mg and
800 mg were safe and more efficacious than placebo at reducing cannabis use.

previous case reports22,23 and reduced anxiety symptoms in line with experimental studies in humans28 and rats.29 Key strengths of this study include its novel indication for which there is substantial clinical need, and its adaptive Bayesian dose-finding design.
